######## framework--early-history-of-periodisation-kotov-to-dyson
     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: framework
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "6.1"
     7	topic: history of periodisation
     8	category: [periodization, history, annual-plan, transition-phase]
     9	confidence: supported
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-03
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Early History of Periodisation: From Kotov's Three Stages to Dyson's Five Phases
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors trace training organisation from ancient practice to the first formal periodisation schemes (PDF p. 324-325 / printed p. 313-314, verified against the page images):
    17	- Ancient Greeks prepared for the Olympic Games with "a preparatory training period of at least 10 months a year" (PDF p. 324 / printed p. 313).
    18	- Kotov (*Olympic Sport*, 1917) divided training into general, preparatory and specific stages: the general stage developed the "vegetative (cardiovascular-respiratory) and muscular systems"; preparatory training of "about two months' duration" improved strength and muscle endurance; the specific stage had initial and main parts "both of about four months' duration," but "there was still no overall methodology of periodisation in the form of definite cycles" (PDF p. 324 / printed p. 313).
    19	- Gorinewsky (1922) and Birsin (1925) took "preliminary steps"; sport-specific applications followed in 1938-1940 (track and field, skiing, gymnastics, boxing, water sports).
    20	- Pikhala (*Athletism*, Finland, 1930) used "an undulating rhythm of training which alternates periods of work and rest" to prevent overtraining, but planned around "climatic seasons, rather than quantitatively determined phases of loading."
    21	- Grantyn (1939) split the year into preparatory, main and transitional periods, the transition being "a gradual detraining to rest, followed by active rest" with other sports such as gymnastics and jogging, which the authors call an early form of "combinational training" as restoration.
    22	- Ozolin (1949) stressed the competition calendar and climate, and active rest within the transition phase.
    23	- Letunov (1950) "strongly criticised the formulation of training regimes on the basis of the competition calendar alone," holding that stages follow biological processes, though "he failed to appreciate that these processes, in turn, were modified by the training loads" (PDF p. 325 / printed p. 314).
    24	- Dyson (*A New System of Training*, England, 1946) gave a five-phase athletics year: non-competitive preparation (5 months), pre-competitive (1 month), initial competitive (6 weeks), main competitive (6 weeks), post-competitive (6 weeks) (PDF p. 325 / printed p. 314).
    25	
    26	**Why it works** — This is a historical account, not a mechanism. The authors' through-line is that organisation moved from seasons and calendars toward phases set by biological adaptation, and they fault Letunov for missing that the loads themselves change those biological processes (PDF p. 325 / printed p. 314).
    27	
    28	**When to apply** — When explaining to staff or students where macro, meso and microcycle language came from, or when an older Russian or British source uses phase names that do not match current terms. Eric's baseline: "Macro/meso/microcycle structure is used as the standard planning language" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 179, Inferred (transcript + slides)).
    29	
    30	**When NOT to apply** — Not evidence that any one historical scheme works: the authors give no outcome data for Kotov, Grantyn or Dyson. Pikhala's "undulating rhythm" (1930) is about alternating work and rest, and is not the same thing as the modern undulating (daily or weekly varied) resistance model; Inference: do not cite it as an origin of that model without checking Pikhala. The authors themselves warn on the next page that this history "may create the impression that periodisation is the only type of organisation," which they call "far from the truth" (PDF p. 325 / printed p. 314).
    31	
    32	**Example** — The authors' own: Dyson's 1946 athletics year, 5 months of non-competitive preparation with "gym training and cross-country running," then 1 month of pre-competitive specific preparation, then three 6-week blocks (initial competitive, main competitive, post-competitive) (PDF p. 325 / printed p. 314).
    33	
    34	**Related** — [[claim--seasonal-trainability-hettinger-muller-ultraviolet]], [[framework--sport-alone-vs-sport-plus-supplementary-training-and-adjunct-modes]], [[framework--training-cycle-hierarchy-durations-and-russian-term-swap]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--evans-history-lineage-of-sport-science-giants]], [[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas]]
######## heuristic--progress-skills-only-at-70-80-percent-technical-reliability
     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: heuristic
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "6.2"
     7	topic: reliability of technique
     8	category: [technique, skill-acquisition, monitoring, progression, competition-stress]
     9	confidence: supported
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-03
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Track Reliability of Technique, and Progress Only When It Has Stabilised at 70-80% or Better
    15	
    16	**What it is** — "Even the most meticulous computation and prescription of load intensity, volume and sequencing ... is of little consequence to performance if changes in technical mastery are not constantly monitored." Lab tests "simply identify the potential offered by the athlete's work capacity and not functional preparedness" (PDF p. 329 / printed p. 318, verified against the page image). The tool is *reliability of technique*: the percentage of successes in executing the same specific skills, kept separately for training and competition. "A low competitive reliability relative to training reliability indicates that the athlete probably has difficulty in performing under conditions of high emotional excitement and needs to simulate those conditions during training"; "gym lifters" lift much more in training than on the platform, where emotional stress affects "not ... the obviously adequate levels of strength or power, but ... the technical skills required." Rule: "Progression to more difficult skills should not occur until the reliability at the preceding level of complexity or intensity has stabilised at a level of at least 70-80%," the "*zone-by-zone mastering of intensity* (Matveyev, 1977)." Technical-training dose is steered by a *feedforward method* ("the quantitatively planned long-term scheme") and a *feedback method* ("the ad hoc daily approach") because technical emphasis "can fluctuate rapidly" (PDF p. 330 / printed p. 319, verified against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning: performance depends on "functional preparedness, which relies on the mastery of specific motor skills," and "loss of form is prematurely attributed to overtraining or deficient training" when the real problem is inadequate monitoring and cyclical variation of skills training (PDF p. 329-330 / printed p. 318-319).
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — Any skill progression with a clear success criterion (a lift made, a drill rep executed to standard). Inference: `docs/method-baseline.md` records no explicit technique-reliability metric, so this is a gap the passage could fill. The authors later add a coach-scored Rating of Technique column to the session log (PDF p. 339 / printed p. 328; see [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]]).
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The 70-80% threshold has no cited data beyond the Matveyev label, and it needs "zones of intensity or complexity" to be "formally laid down for each aspect of a given sport" first. Inference: in open, reactive team-sport skills a success rate is harder to define than in a weightlifting attempt, so the threshold transfers best to closed skills. Inference: the third bullet in the source list ("the premature introduction of skills") reads as a factor to avoid, not one to stress; the source wording is ambiguous.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own: the "gym lifter" whose training lifts far exceed platform lifts, read as a technical and emotional problem rather than a strength deficit (PDF p. 329 / printed p. 318).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]], [[heuristic--keep-event-specific-competitive-stress-in-preparation]], [[framework--eight-weaknesses-of-the-matveyev-model]], [[claim--plyometric-skill-is-cognitive-and-state-dependent]]
######## framework--volume-intensity-and-relative-intensity-calculation
     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: framework
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "6.2.2"
     7	topic: volume and intensity calculation
     8	category: [periodization, load-monitoring, volume-load, relative-intensity, training-log]
     9	confidence: supported
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-03
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Calculating Volume, Mean Intensity and Relative Intensity, and Why Averages Mislead
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Volume is "intended to provide some measure of the total work done over a given period and intensity is a measure of the average force exerted"; approximate measures replace "the precise methods of physics" (PDF p. 334 / printed p. 323, verified against the page image).
    17	- **Volume** of an exercise (kg) = weight x repetitions; workout volume = sum over "all the major exercises."
    18	- **Number of lifts** = total repetitions.
    19	- **Intensity** of an exercise = its volume / its repetitions; workout intensity = total volume / total lifts, "the average weight lifted."
    20	- **Relative intensity** = intensity / 1RM x 100, "usually more meaningful."
    21	- Exclusions: "Some authorities (Chernyak, 1978) stipulate that only weights of greater than 40% of 1RM should be taken into account ... since the strengthening effects of lighter weights than this is minimal." Then: "Generally, except for beginners, warmup sets with loads of less than about 70% of 1RM are not included in the calculations."
    22	- Near-misses count: "if a weightlifter manages to raise a snatch or jerk above the head, but fails to complete the lift, then the attempt is counted" (PDF p. 335 / printed p. 324).
    23	- Hybrid exercises (e.g. 100 kg power clean x2 + front squat x3 + push press x1) are written as 100 over 2+3+1, volume 600 kg (PDF p. 336 / printed p. 325, verified against the page image).
    24	- Some, such as Medvedev (1989), prefer number of lifts alone, since computed averages let "a few sets of lighter loads ... swamp the effect of a small number of maximal efforts" (PDF p. 336 / printed p. 325).
    25	
    26	**Why it works** — The authors' warning about averages: "the use of overall averages can be very misleading in prescribing training, since they give no indication of the range of loads used ... Thus, the overall demands of training must always be examined simultaneously in terms of intensity and volume" (PDF p. 334 / printed p. 323).
    27	
    28	**When to apply** — Any weight-room load log or dashboard that reports tonnage or average load. Eric's baseline: "Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)); the baseline adds an Inference that "with no true 1RM testing (Q10), any %1RM prescription rests on projected maxes." Inference: the same caveat applies to relative intensity computed here.
    29	
    30	**When NOT to apply** — Two exclusion thresholds sit on the same page and are not reconciled: Chernyak's "greater than 40% of 1RM" and the general "less than about 70% of 1RM" warm-up exclusion; the worked example drops a 50% set as a warm-up, which follows the 70% rule. Record which rule a log uses. The method covers barbell lifts; the authors log jumps separately by height and repetitions (PDF p. 336 / printed p. 325). Small-muscle exercises are usually excluded, but the authors warn this can hide fatigue (PDF p. 340; see [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]]).
    31	
    32	**Example** — The authors' own: Exercise A, 60 kg x 10, 80 kg x 8, 100 kg x 4, 110 kg x 2, 1RM 120 kg. The 60 kg set (50%) is dropped as a warm-up. Volume = 640 + 400 + 220 = 1260 kg; reps = 14; intensity = 1260 / 14 = 90 kg; relative intensity = 90 / 120 x 100 = 75%. Yet the top set was 110 kg (92%), and "The same relative intensity could be achieved by executing 3 identical sets each with 75kg for 3 repetitions," which "would be far less demanding" (PDF p. 334 / printed p. 323). Inference: 3 x 3 at 75 kg is 62.5% of 120 kg, not 75%; the sentence only works if it means 90 kg, so treat that comparison as a printing slip.
    33	
    34	**Related** — [[framework--intensity-zone-distribution-and-load-recording]], [[claim--vorobyev-mean-training-weight-by-bodymass-and-qualification]], [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/heuristic--intensity-defines-target-volume-defines-depth]]

    14	# Calculating Volume, Mean Intensity and Relative Intensity, and Why Averages Mislead
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Volume is "intended to provide some measure of the total work done over a given period and intensity is a measure of the average force exerted"; approximate measures replace "the precise methods of physics" (PDF p. 334 / printed p. 323, verified against the page image).
    17	- **Volume** of an exercise (kg) = weight x repetitions; workout volume = sum over "all the major exercises."
    18	- **Number of lifts** = total repetitions.
    19	- **Intensity** of an exercise = its volume / its repetitions; workout intensity = total volume / total lifts, "the average weight lifted."
    20	- **Relative intensity** = intensity / 1RM x 100, "usually more meaningful."
    21	- Exclusions: "Some authorities (Chernyak, 1978) stipulate that only weights of greater than 40% of 1RM should be taken into account ... since the strengthening effects of lighter weights than this is minimal." Then: "Generally, except for beginners, warmup sets with loads of less than about 70% of 1RM are not included in the calculations."
    22	- Near-misses count: "if a weightlifter manages to raise a snatch or jerk above the head, but fails to complete the lift, then the attempt is counted" (PDF p. 335 / printed p. 324).
    23	- Hybrid exercises (e.g. 100 kg power clean x2 + front squat x3 + push press x1) are written as 100 over 2+3+1, volume 600 kg (PDF p. 336 / printed p. 325, verified against the page image).
    24	- Some, such as Medvedev (1989), prefer number of lifts alone, since computed averages let "a few sets of lighter loads ... swamp the effect of a small number of maximal efforts" (PDF p. 336 / printed p. 325).
    25	
    26	**Why it works** — The authors' warning about averages: "the use of overall averages can be very misleading in prescribing training, since they give no indication of the range of loads used ... Thus, the overall demands of training must always be examined simultaneously in terms of intensity and volume" (PDF p. 334 / printed p. 323).
    27	
    28	**When to apply** — Any weight-room load log or dashboard that reports tonnage or average load. Eric's baseline: "Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)); the baseline adds an Inference that "with no true 1RM testing (Q10), any %1RM prescription rests on projected maxes." Inference: the same caveat applies to relative intensity computed here.
    29	
    30	**When NOT to apply** — Two exclusion thresholds sit on the same page and are not reconciled: Chernyak's "greater than 40% of 1RM" and the general "less than about 70% of 1RM" warm-up exclusion; the worked example drops a 50% set as a warm-up, which follows the 70% rule. Record which rule a log uses. The method covers barbell lifts; the authors log jumps separately by height and repetitions (PDF p. 336 / printed p. 325). Small-muscle exercises are usually excluded, but the authors warn this can hide fatigue (PDF p. 340; see [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]]).
    31	
    32	**Example** — The authors' own: Exercise A, 60 kg x 10, 80 kg x 8, 100 kg x 4, 110 kg x 2, 1RM 120 kg. The 60 kg set (50%) is dropped as a warm-up. Volume = 640 + 400 + 220 = 1260 kg; reps = 14; intensity = 1260 / 14 = 90 kg; relative intensity = 90 / 120 x 100 = 75%. Yet the top set was 110 kg (92%), and "The same relative intensity could be achieved by executing 3 identical sets each with 75kg for 3 repetitions," which "would be far less demanding" (PDF p. 334 / printed p. 323). Inference: 3 x 3 at 75 kg is 62.5% of 120 kg, not 75%; the sentence only works if it means 90 kg, so treat that comparison as a printing slip.
    33	
    34	**Related** — [[framework--intensity-zone-distribution-and-load-recording]], [[claim--vorobyev-mean-training-weight-by-bodymass-and-qualification]], [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/heuristic--intensity-defines-target-volume-defines-depth]]

######## framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique
     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: framework
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "6.2.2"
     7	topic: cybernetic periodisation
     8	category: [periodization, autoregulation, rpe, monitoring, technique]
     9	confidence: supported
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-03
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Cybernetic Periodisation: Steer the Preplanned Scheme With RPE and a Rating of Technique
    15	
    16	**What it is** — "The use of numerical computations as the sole descriptor of loading often overlooks ... the athlete's *subjective perception of the intensity and overall effects of the loading*." Bulgarian weightlifting answered this with a method "which required athletes always to train at a perceived maximum load" (PDF p. 339 / printed p. 328, verified against the page image). The proposal:
    17	- Add an RPE column ("Rating of Perceived Effort") on a 1-3 (light, medium, heavy), 1-10, or "most popular" 1-5 scale. "You do not record an RPE for every repetition or exercise, but note it mentally in each set and use it to guide you in your next set. At the end of the workout, you then record only the RPE for the heaviest or most demanding sets."
    18	- RPE "usually be used to identify any decrease rather than an increase in actual load."
    19	- Add a coach-scored Rating of Technique (RT) for the most demanding efforts, with video if more validity is needed (Table 6.4).
    20	- Plot intensities, volumes, actual performances and RPEs on the same axes over time.
    21	
    22	"This modified form of periodisation may be known as *cybernetic periodisation*, since the original preplanned periodisation scheme is regularly modified by subjective and objective feedback obtained from the lifter's current performance state" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329, verified against the page image), after Wiener (1948). "Traditional periodisation can often prove to be as limited as non-periodised training, since all loading is based upon a fixed original input." It is "a quantified extension of what may be termed intuitive training." The Bulgarian "method of maximum effort": if the top lift "felt very demanding, the lifter might decrease the load by 10kg and perform a few sets of no more than 2 repetitions with it, and then follow this with an increase of 5kg for another few single attempts." Two side rules: periodically include minor exercises (calf raises, elbow curls, lat pulldowns) in calculations, since excluding them "might disguise the fact that they are fatiguing some muscle groups," and avoid placing them randomly before major lifts; and use RPE and RT to adjust for heavy loading from the athlete's job, "most significant in the case of heavy manual labourers" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329).
    23	
    24	**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "the athlete responds to any exercise in terms of how the load feels at any given moment or period, rather than mechanically according to some numerical computation" (PDF p. 339 / printed p. 328); and "Over-reliance on numerical computations ... is a major reason why some coaches tend to dismiss their relevance" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329). Voice, Inference: the cybernetic-periodisation label and this section read as Siff's own contribution (Section 6.3 refers back to it as what "this textbook introduced," PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334); the book does not attribute it to Verkhoshansky.
    25	
    26	**When to apply** — Whenever a percentage-based plan runs on projected rather than tested maxes. Eric's baseline: Prilepin's chart is the default rep/set guide, with the baseline's own Inference that "with no true 1RM testing (Q10), any %1RM prescription rests on projected maxes" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)). Inference: RPE-guided downward adjustment is the authors' safeguard for exactly that case. For hard practice days in football, the "normal daily job" point applies by analogy to practice load before a lift (Inference).
    27	
    28	**When NOT to apply** — The authors advise RPE mainly to reduce load, not to push it up. The 10 kg down, 5 kg up rule is a Bulgarian elite weightlifting example, not a general prescription. This entry overlaps with the authors' APRE in 5.2.2, which adjusts load by repetitions achieved rather than by perception ([[framework--apre-autoregulating-progressive-resistance-exercise]]); the two are compatible but separate tools. Issurin maps workout load onto Borg RPE bands on a different scale ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]]); do not mix the scales.
    29	
    30	**Example** — The authors' own: a Bulgarian lifter whose maximum attempt feels very demanding drops 10 kg for a few sets of at most 2 reps, then adds 5 kg for a few singles (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329).
    31	
    32	**Related** — [[framework--apre-autoregulating-progressive-resistance-exercise]], [[heuristic--progress-skills-only-at-70-80-percent-technical-reliability]], [[framework--volume-intensity-and-relative-intensity-calculation]], [[claim--periodisation-controversy-verkhoshansky-vs-zheljazkov]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]]
######## heuristic--heart-rate-work-capacity-tests-for-lifters
     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: heuristic
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "6.2.2"
     7	topic: heart-rate work capacity tests
     8	category: [monitoring, heart-rate, work-capacity, weightlifting, testing]
     9	confidence: supported
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-03
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Heart-Rate Work-Capacity Tests for Lifters: the Novik Squat Test and an Adapted PWC-170
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Heart rate can show what load computations miss: "If the heart rate increases noticeably prior to the heavier or heaviest training loads in any session, it indicates the presence of significant levels of emotional arousal and a more demanding level of training intensity, even though the periodisation computations might indicate otherwise" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329, verified against the page image). Measure HR before, immediately after, and each minute for 4 minutes after an exercise; for resistance training, take recovery HR after "repetition squats, cleans and bench press" rather than on a treadmill, "because of the effects such as local muscle ischaemia."
    17	- **Novik squat test** (Novik et al, 1980, Olympic weightlifters): at the start of a cycle, find the 1RM squat; then do "one set of 3 repetitions of squats" at "85-90% of this 1RM," and measure HR "for a period lasting one minute." Repeat through the cycle: "If the immediate post-squatting and the post-one minute heart rates decrease, then work capacity has increased and loading may be increased" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329).
    18	- **Adapted PWC-170** (Karpman et al, 1982; Dvorkin, 1988), PDF p. 341 / printed p. 330, verified against the page image: with the 10RM load, rest about 5 minutes, do 5 reps, measure HR (F1); rest another 5 minutes, do 8-10 reps, measure HR (F2). PWC-170 = N1 + (N2 - N1)(170 - F1)/(F2 - F1), where N = 9.8 x W x R x D, and D is the bar distance as a fraction of lifter height H (Table 6.5). The squat "is far more commonly used." Table 6.5 values (concentric D / equivalent D for total work): full back squat 0.35 H / 0.60 H; half squat 0.22 / 0.37; bench press 0.28 / 0.56; squat clean 0.67 / 1.26; split clean 0.55 / 0.77; clean pull 0.50 / 0.50; snatch pull 0.59 / 0.59; power clean 0.65 / 0.69; deep good morning 0.35 / 0.52; jerk from chest 0.54 / 0.60; split snatch 0.67 / 0.89.
    19	
    20	**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning: a lower HR response to the same submaximal squat effort means higher work capacity (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329). No physiological explanation beyond that is given.
    21	
    22	**When to apply** — As a low-cost in-house readiness and capacity check during a strength block, using an exercise athletes already do. Inference: no line in `docs/method-baseline.md` describes a lift-specific heart-rate response, so the Novik test would add to Baylor's force-plate and GPS monitoring rather than replace any of it.
    23	
    24	**When NOT to apply** — The Novik test requires a measured 1RM squat, which the baseline says is not routinely tested (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material), citing Q10). Table 6.5 is not internally consistent with its own note: the text says eccentric action was "estimated to add 70% more work in each case where there is significant eccentric action," but the table's ratios differ (Inference from the printed values: back squat about +71%, bench press +100%, squat clean about +88%, power clean about +6%, pulls 0%). The book does not explain the variation. HR is also raised by "emotional arousal," so a high reading does not by itself separate fatigue from nerves.
    25	
    26	**Example** — The authors' own: a weightlifter squats 3 reps at 85-90% of 1RM at intervals through a cycle; falling immediate and 1-minute post-set HR signals higher work capacity and permits more load (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329).
    27	
    28	**Related** — [[framework--supplementary-readiness-markers-hr-bp-ceff-palpation]], [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]], [[claim--vorobyev-mean-training-weight-by-bodymass-and-qualification]], [[research-papers/thorpe-2017-monitoring-fatigue-status-in-elite-team-sport-athletes-implications-for-practice]]
######## claim--periodisation-controversy-verkhoshansky-vs-zheljazkov
     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: claim
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "6.3"
     7	topic: the periodisation controversy
     8	category: [periodization, matveyev, critique, elite-athletes, evidence-quality]
     9	confidence: contested
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-03
    12	---
    13	
    14	# The Periodisation Controversy: Verkhoshansky's Critique of Classical Periodisation and Zheljazkov's Reply
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Section 6.3 (PDF p. 344-346 / printed p. 333-335; verified against the page images) is Siff's voice by the book's own signals: it names Verkhoshansky in the third person throughout and refers to what "this textbook introduced." It has three voices.
    17	
    18	**Siff's framing.** Classical Matveyev periodisation is widely used in the West, yet "even among Russian researchers and scientists, this approach to training has attracted some fierce criticism." Siff accepts part of it: the belief that periodisation is "an exact science" with computerised prescriptions is wrong, because "The body is not an exactly controlled, deterministic system"; training is "as much a matter of art, trial-and-error, and intuition, as it is of science," so schemes "should serve as approximate guidelines" modified by physiological and psychological markers (PDF p. 344 / printed p. 333). He concludes "organising training according to the classical model of Matveyev can be used only by athletes of low qualification for certain phases of the programme," the reason the book introduced ongoing subjective and objective assessment (PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334). He also objects that classical computation "utilises only two factors," volume and intensity.
    19	
    20	**Verkhoshansky (1997), as reported by Siff.** Periodisation "is not a suitable model for training for elite sportsmen" and should be "rejected or modified" for modern crowded calendars; "at best, separate forms of periodisation should be used by novice and young athletes." The mechanical division into periods and mesocycles rests on 1950s Soviet experience "mainly on the example of three sports, namely swimming, weightlifting, track and field athletics." Training should rest "much more on physiology." Plans should meet demands "distributed throughout a competitive season" rather than "notorious peaks of sports form." Kenyan runners "have never implemented periodisation"; British runners declined after adopting "Matveyev's block scheme" widely after 1980 (citing Horwill 1992, 1995; Tschiene 1991, 1992). He rejects "laws" of training and dismisses "'undulating models and 'wave models'" as "word play" (PDF p. 344-345 / printed p. 333-334).
    21	
    22	**Zheljazkov (1998), as reported by Siff.** Periodisation "still managed to be utilised very effectively for many years in training numerous elite soviet and Eastern European athletes"; it is "erroneous" to treat Matveyev's concept as "the complete theory of sports training"; Verkhoshansky's charges of "primitive methodology" and "scholastic demagogy" are "a unprofessional personal attack"; national rises and falls in running are natural, not caused by periodisation. Classical periodisation "has not lost its fundamental importance" but has "serious qualitative limitations" to be modified by research on "exhaustion, adaptation and restoration," since regeneration is "nonlinear and heterochronical"; applied sport science "does not at all replace the entire concept of periodisation, but enriches it" (PDF p. 345-346 / printed p. 334-335).
    23	
    24	**Why it works** — Each side argues from different evidence: Verkhoshansky from the 1950s origins of the model, its three-sport base and national running records; Zheljazkov from decades of Soviet and Eastern European elite success. Neither gives controlled data on these pages, and both national-results arguments are correlational (Inference).
    25	
    26	**When to apply** — When a plan treats the annual chart as fixed. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred (transcript)), and "in football you want to peak every Saturday" (line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: both sides would accept the roadmap framing, and Verkhoshansky's season-long demands point fits weekly football games better than a single peak.
    27	
    28	**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** Same question (is classical periodisation suitable for elite athletes), two named authorities, opposite answers, on PDF p. 344 versus p. 345. Note the internal tension with the book's own method: Verkhoshansky dismisses "undulating models" as word play (PDF p. 345), while the authors endorse heavy, medium and light alternation (PDF p. 326, 329); Inference: his complaint is about relabelling, not about load variation working, so it is a tension in emphasis, not a contradiction. This also touches Eric's baseline directly: "Undulating/non-linear periodization ... is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression" (line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Library sources: Issurin 2016 judged evidence for Verkhoshansky's own concentrated-unidirectional alternative insufficient for team sports ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]); Harries et al. 2015 found linear and undulating programmes give similar strength gains, and Afonso et al. 2019 argue that periodised-versus-non-periodised meta-analyses did not isolate periodisation's effect (vault research-papers entries). Inference: the modern papers support neither side's strong claim. Evans frames the same split as "classic" versus "non-classic" literature ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--periodization-evidence-classic-vs-nonclassic-literature-debate]]).
    29	
    30	**Example** — The authors' own: Verkhoshansky's claim that British middle-distance runners won Olympic gold before, not after, adopting Matveyev's scheme widely after 1980, against Zheljazkov's reply that "all sports in all nations naturally undergo periods of ascendancy and decline" (PDF p. 344-345 / printed p. 333-334).

    16	**What it is** — Heart rate can show what load computations miss: "If the heart rate increases noticeably prior to the heavier or heaviest training loads in any session, it indicates the presence of significant levels of emotional arousal and a more demanding level of training intensity, even though the periodisation computations might indicate otherwise" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329, verified against the page image). Measure HR before, immediately after, and each minute for 4 minutes after an exercise; for resistance training, take recovery HR after "repetition squats, cleans and bench press" rather than on a treadmill, "because of the effects such as local muscle ischaemia."
    17	- **Novik squat test** (Novik et al, 1980, Olympic weightlifters): at the start of a cycle, find the 1RM squat; then do "one set of 3 repetitions of squats" at "85-90% of this 1RM," and measure HR "for a period lasting one minute." Repeat through the cycle: "If the immediate post-squatting and the post-one minute heart rates decrease, then work capacity has increased and loading may be increased" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329).
    18	- **Adapted PWC-170** (Karpman et al, 1982; Dvorkin, 1988), PDF p. 341 / printed p. 330, verified against the page image: with the 10RM load, rest about 5 minutes, do 5 reps, measure HR (F1); rest another 5 minutes, do 8-10 reps, measure HR (F2). PWC-170 = N1 + (N2 - N1)(170 - F1)/(F2 - F1), where N = 9.8 x W x R x D, and D is the bar distance as a fraction of lifter height H (Table 6.5). The squat "is far more commonly used."     15	
    16	**What it is** — Section 6.3 (PDF p. 344-346 / printed p. 333-335; verified against the page images) is Siff's voice by the book's own signals: it names Verkhoshansky in the third person throughout and refers to what "this textbook introduced." It has three voices.
    17	
    18	**Siff's framing.** Classical Matveyev periodisation is widely used in the West, yet "even among Russian researchers and scientists, this approach to training has attracted some fierce criticism." Siff accepts part of it: the belief that periodisation is "an exact science" with computerised prescriptions is wrong, because "The body is not an exactly controlled, deterministic system"; training is "as much a matter of art, trial-and-error, and intuition, as it is of science," so schemes "should serve as approximate guidelines" modified by physiological and psychological markers (PDF p. 344 / printed p. 333). He concludes "organising training according to the classical model of Matveyev can be used only by athletes of low qualification for certain phases of the programme," the reason the book introduced ongoing subjective and objective assessment (PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334). He also objects that classical computation "utilises only two factors," volume and intensity.
    19	
    20	**Verkhoshansky (1997), as reported by Siff.** Periodisation "is not a suitable model for training for elite sportsmen" and should be "rejected or modified" for modern crowded calendars; "at best, separate forms of periodisation should be used by novice and young athletes." 6.3 The Periodisation Controversy
The widespread Western use of classical periodisation along the lines originally pioneered by Matveyev may 
create the impression that it should be regarded as the pre-eminent and most appropriate method of organising 
long term training. 
However, even among Russian researchers and scientists, this approach to training has 
attracted some fierce criticism.
Some of this criticism is warranted, such as the belief that periodisation is an exact science in which all 
training may be prescribed via the use of computerised programmes based upon exact calculations of intensity 
and volume of every training session, microcycle and longer term cycle. The body is not an exactly controlled, 
deterministic system, but its subsystems are attracted to and deviate from approximate states of balance which 
show continual variation to ensure long term efficiency and health, as is being confirmed by more and more 
research into the nature of fractal, chaotic or frizzy processes in biology (see Ch 8). The organisation of training 
is ais much a matter of art, trial-and-error, and intuition, as it is of science, so that periodisation schemes should 
serve as approximate guidelines to be followed and modified by ongoing analysis of various physiological and 
psychological markers of progress. Some of the methods, such as ratings of perceived effort, which may be used 
to provide fine tuning of periodisation schemes were discussed in the sections immediately preceding this one.
Verkhoshansky (1997), in particular, has roundly criticised texts which extol so-called ‘periodisation 
breakthroughs’, stating that the material being offered as an exact science is setting back the progress of training 
organisation to the era of the 1950s. He stresses that periodisation is not a suitable model for training for elite 
sportsmen and should be rejected or modified according to trends in the very full calendars of world sports which 
involve far more competition at higher levels than when the concept of periodisation was first formulated. Thus, 
at best, separate forms of periodisation should be used by novice and young athletes.
He points out that the typical mechanical division of annual training into periods and mesocycles has been 
based on the short-term experience of preparation of athletes during the early stage of formulating the Soviet 
system of training (of the 1950s) and mainly on the example of three sports, namely swimming, weightlifting, 
track and field athletics, and therefore cannot be universally applied in its basic form. It is emphasized, that any 
system of training should be based not so much on logic and empirical experience, but much more on physiology.
Verkhoshansky (1997) considers that Russian experts in cyclic sports, guided by pcriodisation, have applied 
outdated training methods which for many years have retarded sporting progress. He states that such a procedure 
is insufficiently scientifically substantiated and is not capable of providing accurate long-term preparation of 
athletes. Plans to produce high results should not be based on training to achieve what he terms “notorious peaks 
of sports form”, but should meet the ongoing demands of events distributed throughout a competitive season and 
not simply to produce performance peaks for a very few events.
In his critique, Verkhoshansky (1997) makes specific reference to distance running. He emphasizes that the 
very successful African athletes, especially the Kenyans, train in mountainous terrain and have certain genetic 
and cultural predispositions, as confirmed by Soviet experts, and that they have never implemented periodisation 
in their training. He adds that African and European athletes should not imitate one another, even if impressive 
results may tempt athletes to do so. He also refers to articles by Horwill (1992, 1995) on the same topic which 
condemn "the slavish worship of the theory of periodisation as used by some runners in different countries”. He 
stresses that Soviet runners did not improve world records in running middle distances and the British runners 
who used the Russian concept of periodisation did not gain gold medals on Olympic games over the last 30 years, 
but produced great achievements before they used such concepts. British runners started to use Matveyev’s block 
scheme of periodisation widely after 1980 and from then on their results showed a disturbing tendency to declinc.
Verkhoshansky citcs the work of Tschiene (1991, 1992) who has analysed a number of present training 
concepts to conclude that periodisation has not changed from the moment of Matveyev’s first formalisation of the 
topic in 1965. 
Although the nature of major sports and scientific achievements have progressed greatly since 
those early days, Tschiene observes that many coach's doctrines have not advanced or given way to other more 
progressive approaches.
Several critics of classical periodisation stress the artificiality and clumsiness of classifying the various 
microcyclcs and mesocyclcs in the form of an exact number of days or weeks, as well as the dubious linear 
stringing together of fairly arbitrary, non-linear, non-discrete building blocks of subjectively chosen exercises.

For instance, the use of an unloading microcycle in a given mesocycle while the body of the athlete is in a state 
of supercompensation docs not take into account the sometimes random and unpredictable effects of average and 
small waves of loads on the body. 
As a result, it needs to be stressed that organising training according to the 
classical model of Matveyev can be used only by athletes of low qualification for certain phases of the 
programme. 
This is a major reason why this textbook introduced the use o f methods based upon ongoing 
subjective and objective assessment of the athlete’s condition.
Vcrkhoshansky (1997) is especially critical of any periodisation texts which confuse the meaning of "law’, 
"principles”, "fundamentals" and so forth, because of the lack of adequate scicntific research to support such 
notions. He feels that much of the terminology represents a thinly veiled attempt to create a greater aura of 
authenticity to the host of periodisation schemes that flow from the pens of many authors and coaches, especially 
in the West, without their being able to scientifically validate their creations. He stresses that with respect to 
advanced physical training, there are no ‘laws’ in the rigorous sense of this word. Similarly, he dismisses as word 
play the use of terms such as 'undulating models and ‘wave models’ as meaningless attempts to disguise 
pcriodisation in different language, without changing the status quo in the least.
He makes the interesting observation that many Westerners seem to be oblivious of the fact that the general 
paradigm of periodisation was based heavily upon the philosophies and methodologies of communism. The 
cyclical nature of pcriodisation was strongly influenced by the ‘five year plans' and other cyclcs of productivity in 
the soviet system, while the precise calculation of training quantities reflected attempts to minimise the 
unscicntific factors of subjectivity and emotiveness.
An issue that is also of real concern is the fact that classical computation of periodisation training schemes 
generally utilises only two factors in regulating the training of the athlete, namely the volume and intensity of the 
training load. This is one reason why this book paid special attention to Matveyev’s attempt to include technkal 
skill training as one of the factors involved in periodisation, as well as to models such as that of Bondarchuk, who 
stressed the interdependence of technique and load throughout the training process. Mention was also made earlier 
of the value of prescribing training in terms of zones of intensity and various perceived ratings of technique, effort 
and fatigue to overcome the limits of classical periodisation (see the section on Cybernetic Periodisation).
Some of Verkhoshansky’s criticism have been countered by the Bulgarian scientist, Zheljazkov (1998), who 
considers that the concept of periodisation, however empirical and simplistic it may have been for much of its 
history, still managed to be utilised very effectively for many years in training numerous elite soviet and Eastern 
European athletes in many sports. He comments that it is erroneous for anyone, including Vcrkhoshansky, to 
consider Matveyev's concept of periodisation as being the complete theory of sports training in the preparation, 
bccausc this was not the aim of its author. He does not accept the judgement that it has played a negative role in 
the field of elite sports preparation, becausc he feels that the outstanding achievements of athletes of the former 
Soviet Union vigorously disprove this point of view. 
He considers that Verkhoshansky's emotional conclusions 
that the theory of periodization is constructed on ‘primitive methodology’ and ‘scholastic demagogy* constitute a 
unprofessional personal attack on Matveyev. He disagrees that the crisis in cyclic sports and loss of progress by 
athletes in certain countries in running and track and field athletics are due to the ‘ill-starred’ classical theory of 
periodization by Matveyev, bccausc all sports in all nations naturally undergo periods of ascendancy and decline. 
He agrees that models of society such as communism indeed have a profound impact on the nature of sports 
training, but that this happens in all countries and should not necessarily be taken to mean that this interaction 
between sport and society is always negative.
Zheljazkov (1998) considers that the classical application of periodisation, in describing the varying, phasic 
nature of progress in sporting form, has not lost its fundamental importance, although in the technology of its 
modelling, application and management it exhibits certain serious qualitative limitations, which may be modified 
in the light of modem research and sporting experience. These modifications depend on the effective socialisation 
of sport in any country, the effect of commercialisation and professionalism, the integration of all relevant 
scientific research into training, the development of strong psychological attributes, in athletes, the attachment of 
status to sporting achievement and the application of a more expansive systems theoretical model of the training 
process.
With respect to a systems approach, Zhcljazkov (1998) stresses the importance of using scientific research to 
learn more about the processes of exhaustion, adaptation and restoration so that the methods of training can be 
integrated closely with methods for enhancing adaptation, regeneration and growth under a wide variety of sporting 
conditions. This may then be used to modify classical pcriodisation. He adds that a better knowledge of the 
process of adaptation is very necessary because the dynamics of regeneration, regardless of kind, display a

produced by given tasks, while the criterion of effectiveness lies in its functioning or development. Consequently,

use of strength and motor potential for executing specific motor tasks.

directly contribute to the execution of the motor tasks are important conditions for improving sporting 
proficiency. Therefore, one has to identify the major components of management in sports training, as follows:

create the impression that it should be regarded as the pre-eminent and most appropriate method of organising

and volume of every training session, microcycle and longer term cycle. The body is not an exactly controlled, 
deterministic system, but its subsystems are attracted to and deviate from approximate states of balance which 
show continual variation to ensure long term efficiency and health, as is being confirmed by more and more

serve as approximate guidelines to be followed and modified by ongoing analysis of various physiological and 
psychological markers of progress. Some of the methods, such as ratings of perceived effort, which may be used 
to provide fine tuning of periodisation schemes were discussed in the sections immediately preceding this one.

breakthroughs’, stating that the material being offered as an exact science is setting back the progress of training

track and field athletics, and therefore cannot be universally applied in its basic form. It is emphasized, that any 
system of training should be based not so much on logic and empirical experience, but much more on physiology.

outdated training methods which for many years have retarded sporting progress. He states that such a procedure 
is insufficiently scientifically substantiated and is not capable of providing accurate long-term preparation of 
athletes. Plans to produce high results should not be based on training to achieve what he terms “notorious peaks 
of sports form”, but should meet the ongoing demands of events distributed throughout a competitive season and 
not simply to produce performance peaks for a very few events.

very successful African athletes, especially the Kenyans, train in mountainous terrain and have certain genetic 
and cultural predispositions, as confirmed by Soviet experts, and that they have never implemented periodisation

# Early History of Periodisation: From Kotov's Three Stages to Dyson's Five Phases

**What it is** — The authors trace training organisation from ancient practice to the first formal periodisation schemes (PDF p. 324-325 / printed p. 313-314, verified against the page images):
- Ancient Greeks prepared for the Olympic Games with "a preparatory training period of at least 10 months a year" (PDF p. 324 / printed p. 313).
- Kotov (*Olympic Sport*, 1917) divided training into general, preparatory and specific stages: the general stage developed the "vegetative (cardiovascular-respiratory) and muscular systems"; preparatory training of "about two months' duration" improved strength and muscle endurance; the specific stage had initial and main parts "both of about four months' duration," but "there was still no overall methodology of periodisation in the form of definite cycles" (PDF p. 324 / printed p. 313).
- Gorinewsky (1922) and Birsin (1925) took "preliminary steps"; sport-specific applications followed in 1938-1940 (track and field, skiing, gymnastics, boxing, water sports).
- Pikhala (*Athletism*, Finland, 1930) used "an undulating rhythm of training which alternates periods of work and rest" to prevent overtraining, but planned around "climatic seasons, rather than quantitatively determined phases of loading."
- Grantyn (1939) split the year into preparatory, main and transitional periods, the transition being "a gradual detraining to rest, followed by active rest" with other sports such as gymnastics and jogging, which the authors call an early form of "combinational training" as restoration.
- Ozolin (1949) stressed the competition calendar and climate, and active rest within the transition phase.
- Letunov (1950) "strongly criticised the formulation of training regimes on the basis of the competition calendar alone," holding that stages follow biological processes, though "he failed to appreciate that these processes, in turn, were modified by the training loads" (PDF p. 325 / printed p. 314).
- Dyson (*A New System of Training*, England, 1946) gave a five-phase athletics year: non-competitive preparation (5 months), pre-competitive (1 month), initial competitive (6 weeks), main competitive (6 weeks), post-competitive (6 weeks) (PDF p. 325 / printed p. 314).

**Why it works** — This is a historical account, not a mechanism. The authors' through-line is that organisation moved from seasons and calendars toward phases set by biological adaptation, and they fault Letunov for missing that the loads themselves change those biological processes (PDF p. 325 / printed p. 314).

**When to apply** — When explaining to staff or students where macro, meso and microcycle language came from, or when an older Russian or British source uses phase names that do not match current terms. Eric's baseline: "Macro/meso/microcycle structure is used as the standard planning language" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 179, Inferred (transcript + slides)).

**When NOT to apply** — Not evidence that any one historical scheme works: the authors give no outcome data for Kotov, Grantyn or Dyson. Pikhala's "undulating rhythm" (1930) is about alternating work and rest, and is not the same thing as the modern undulating (daily or weekly varied) resistance model; Inference: do not cite it as an origin of that model without checking Pikhala. The authors themselves warn on the next page that this history "may create the impression that periodisation is the only type of organisation," which they call "far from the truth" (PDF p. 325 / printed p. 314).

**Example** — The authors' own: Dyson's 1946 athletics year, 5 months of non-competitive preparation with "gym training and cross-country running," then 1 month of pre-competitive specific preparation, then three 6-week blocks (initial competitive, main competitive, post-competitive) (PDF p. 325 / printed p. 314).

# Track Reliability of Technique, and Progress Only When It Has Stabilised at 70-80% or Better

**What it is** — "Even the most meticulous computation and prescription of load intensity, volume and sequencing ... is of little consequence to performance if changes in technical mastery are not constantly monitored." Lab tests "simply identify the potential offered by the athlete's work capacity and not functional preparedness" (PDF p. 329 / printed p. 318, verified against the page image). The tool is *reliability of technique*: the percentage of successes in executing the same specific skills, kept separately for training and competition. "A low competitive reliability relative to training reliability indicates that the athlete probably has difficulty in performing under conditions of high emotional excitement and needs to simulate those conditions during training"; "gym lifters" lift much more in training than on the platform, where emotional stress affects "not ... the obviously adequate levels of strength or power, but ... the technical skills required." Rule: "Progression to more difficult skills should not occur until the reliability at the preceding level of complexity or intensity has stabilised at a level of at least 70-80%," the "*zone-by-zone mastering of intensity* (Matveyev, 1977)." Technical-training dose is steered by a *feedforward method* ("the quantitatively planned long-term scheme") and a *feedback method* ("the ad hoc daily approach") because technical emphasis "can fluctuate rapidly" (PDF p. 330 / printed p. 319, verified against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning: performance depends on "functional preparedness, which relies on the mastery of specific motor skills," and "loss of form is prematurely attributed to overtraining or deficient training" when the real problem is inadequate monitoring and cyclical variation of skills training (PDF p. 329-330 / printed p. 318-319).

**When to apply** — Any skill progression with a clear success criterion (a lift made, a drill rep executed to standard). Inference: `docs/method-baseline.md` records no explicit technique-reliability metric, so this is a gap the passage could fill. The authors later add a coach-scored Rating of Technique column to the session log (PDF p. 339 / printed p. 328; see [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The 70-80% threshold has no cited data beyond the Matveyev label, and it needs "zones of intensity or complexity" to be "formally laid down for each aspect of a given sport" first. Inference: in open, reactive team-sport skills a success rate is harder to define than in a weightlifting attempt, so the threshold transfers best to closed skills. Inference: the third bullet in the source list ("the premature introduction of skills") reads as a factor to avoid, not one to stress; the source wording is ambiguous.

**Example** — The authors' own: the "gym lifter" whose training lifts far exceed platform lifts, read as a technical and emotional problem rather than a strength deficit (PDF p. 329 / printed p. 318).

**Related** — [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]], [[heuristic--keep-event-specific-competitive-stress-in-preparation]], [[framework--eight-weaknesses-of-the-matveyev-model]], [[claim--plyometric-skill-is-cognitive-and-state-dependent]]

# Calculating Volume, Mean Intensity and Relative Intensity, and Why Averages Mislead

**What it is** — Volume is "intended to provide some measure of the total work done over a given period and intensity is a measure of the average force exerted"; approximate measures replace "the precise methods of physics" (PDF p. 334 / printed p. 323, verified against the page image).
- **Volume** of an exercise (kg) = weight x repetitions; workout volume = sum over "all the major exercises."
- **Number of lifts** = total repetitions.
- **Intensity** of an exercise = its volume / its repetitions; workout intensity = total volume / total lifts, "the average weight lifted."
- **Relative intensity** = intensity / 1RM x 100, "usually more meaningful."
- Exclusions: "Some authorities (Chernyak, 1978) stipulate that only weights of greater than 40% of 1RM should be taken into account ... since the strengthening effects of lighter weights than this is minimal." Then: "Generally, except for beginners, warmup sets with loads of less than about 70% of 1RM are not included in the calculations."
- Near-misses count: "if a weightlifter manages to raise a snatch or jerk above the head, but fails to complete the lift, then the attempt is counted" (PDF p. 335 / printed p. 324).
- Hybrid exercises (e.g. 100 kg power clean x2 + front squat x3 + push press x1) are written as 100 over 2+3+1, volume 600 kg (PDF p. 336 / printed p. 325, verified against the page image).
- Some, such as Medvedev (1989), prefer number of lifts alone, since computed averages let "a few sets of lighter loads ... swamp the effect of a small number of maximal efforts" (PDF p. 336 / printed p. 325).

**Why it works** — The authors' warning about averages: "the use of overall averages can be very misleading in prescribing training, since they give no indication of the range of loads used ... Thus, the overall demands of training must always be examined simultaneously in terms of intensity and volume" (PDF p. 334 / printed p. 323).

**When to apply** — Any weight-room load log or dashboard that reports tonnage or average load. Eric's baseline: "Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)); the baseline adds an Inference that "with no true 1RM testing (Q10), any %1RM prescription rests on projected maxes." Inference: the same caveat applies to relative intensity computed here.

**When NOT to apply** — Two exclusion thresholds sit on the same page and are not reconciled: Chernyak's "greater than 40% of 1RM" and the general "less than about 70% of 1RM" warm-up exclusion; the worked example drops a 50% set as a warm-up, which follows the 70% rule. Record which rule a log uses. The method covers barbell lifts; the authors log jumps separately by height and repetitions (PDF p. 336 / printed p. 325). Small-muscle exercises are usually excluded, but the authors warn this can hide fatigue (PDF p. 340; see [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]]).

**Example** — The authors' own: Exercise A, 60 kg x 10, 80 kg x 8, 100 kg x 4, 110 kg x 2, 1RM 120 kg. The 60 kg set (50%) is dropped as a warm-up. Volume = 640 + 400 + 220 = 1260 kg; reps = 14; intensity = 1260 / 14 = 90 kg; relative intensity = 90 / 120 x 100 = 75%. Yet the top set was 110 kg (92%), and "The same relative intensity could be achieved by executing 3 identical sets each with 75kg for 3 repetitions," which "would be far less demanding" (PDF p. 334 / printed p. 323). Inference: 3 x 3 at 75 kg is 62.5% of 120 kg, not 75%; the sentence only works if it means 90 kg, so treat that comparison as a printing slip.

**Example** — The authors' own: Exercise A, 60 kg x 10, 80 kg x 8, 100 kg x 4, 110 kg x 2, 1RM 120 kg. The 60 kg set (50%) is dropped as a warm-up. Volume = 640 + 400 + 220 = 1260 kg; reps = 14; intensity = 1260 / 14 = 90 kg; relative intensity = 90 / 120 x 100 = 75%. Yet the top set was 110 kg (92%), and "The same relative intensity could be achieved by executing 3 identical sets each with 75kg for 3 repetitions," which "would be far less demanding" (PDF p. 334 / printed p. 323). Inference: 3 x 3 at 75 kg is 62.5% of 120 kg, not 75%; the sentence only works if it means 90 kg, so treat that comparison as a printing slip.

# Cybernetic Periodisation: Steer the Preplanned Scheme With RPE and a Rating of Technique

**What it is** — "The use of numerical computations as the sole descriptor of loading often overlooks ... the athlete's *subjective perception of the intensity and overall effects of the loading*." Bulgarian weightlifting answered this with a method "which required athletes always to train at a perceived maximum load" (PDF p. 339 / printed p. 328, verified against the page image). The proposal:
- Add an RPE column ("Rating of Perceived Effort") on a 1-3 (light, medium, heavy), 1-10, or "most popular" 1-5 scale. "You do not record an RPE for every repetition or exercise, but note it mentally in each set and use it to guide you in your next set. At the end of the workout, you then record only the RPE for the heaviest or most demanding sets."
- RPE "usually be used to identify any decrease rather than an increase in actual load."
- Add a coach-scored Rating of Technique (RT) for the most demanding efforts, with video if more validity is needed (Table 6.4).
- Plot intensities, volumes, actual performances and RPEs on the same axes over time.

"This modified form of periodisation may be known as *cybernetic periodisation*, since the original preplanned periodisation scheme is regularly modified by subjective and objective feedback obtained from the lifter's current performance state" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329, verified against the page image), after Wiener (1948). "Traditional periodisation can often prove to be as limited as non-periodised training, since all loading is based upon a fixed original input." It is "a quantified extension of what may be termed intuitive training." The Bulgarian "method of maximum effort": if the top lift "felt very demanding, the lifter might decrease the load by 10kg and perform a few sets of no more than 2 repetitions with it, and then follow this with an increase of 5kg for another few single attempts." Two side rules: periodically include minor exercises (calf raises, elbow curls, lat pulldowns) in calculations, since excluding them "might disguise the fact that they are fatiguing some muscle groups," and avoid placing them randomly before major lifts; and use RPE and RT to adjust for heavy loading from the athlete's job, "most significant in the case of heavy manual labourers" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "the athlete responds to any exercise in terms of how the load feels at any given moment or period, rather than mechanically according to some numerical computation" (PDF p. 339 / printed p. 328); and "Over-reliance on numerical computations ... is a major reason why some coaches tend to dismiss their relevance" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329). Voice, Inference: the cybernetic-periodisation label and this section read as Siff's own contribution (Section 6.3 refers back to it as what "this textbook introduced," PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334); the book does not attribute it to Verkhoshansky.

**When to apply** — Whenever a percentage-based plan runs on projected rather than tested maxes. Eric's baseline: Prilepin's chart is the default rep/set guide, with the baseline's own Inference that "with no true 1RM testing (Q10), any %1RM prescription rests on projected maxes" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)). Inference: RPE-guided downward adjustment is the authors' safeguard for exactly that case. For hard practice days in football, the "normal daily job" point applies by analogy to practice load before a lift (Inference).

**When NOT to apply** — The authors advise RPE mainly to reduce load, not to push it up. The 10 kg down, 5 kg up rule is a Bulgarian elite weightlifting example, not a general prescription. This entry overlaps with the authors' APRE in 5.2.2, which adjusts load by repetitions achieved rather than by perception ([[framework--apre-autoregulating-progressive-resistance-exercise]]); the two are compatible but separate tools. Issurin maps workout load onto Borg RPE bands on a different scale ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]]); do not mix the scales.

**Example** — The authors' own: a Bulgarian lifter whose maximum attempt feels very demanding drops 10 kg for a few sets of at most 2 reps, then adds 5 kg for a few singles (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329).

**Related** — [[framework--apre-autoregulating-progressive-resistance-exercise]], [[heuristic--progress-skills-only-at-70-80-percent-technical-reliability]], [[framework--volume-intensity-and-relative-intensity-calculation]], [[claim--periodisation-controversy-verkhoshansky-vs-zheljazkov]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]]

# Heart-Rate Work-Capacity Tests for Lifters: the Novik Squat Test and an Adapted PWC-170

**What it is** — Heart rate can show what load computations miss: "If the heart rate increases noticeably prior to the heavier or heaviest training loads in any session, it indicates the presence of significant levels of emotional arousal and a more demanding level of training intensity, even though the periodisation computations might indicate otherwise" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329, verified against the page image). Measure HR before, immediately after, and each minute for 4 minutes after an exercise; for resistance training, take recovery HR after "repetition squats, cleans and bench press" rather than on a treadmill, "because of the effects such as local muscle ischaemia."
- **Novik squat test** (Novik et al, 1980, Olympic weightlifters): at the start of a cycle, find the 1RM squat; then do "one set of 3 repetitions of squats" at "85-90% of this 1RM," and measure HR "for a period lasting one minute." Repeat through the cycle: "If the immediate post-squatting and the post-one minute heart rates decrease, then work capacity has increased and loading may be increased" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329).
- **Adapted PWC-170** (Karpman et al, 1982; Dvorkin, 1988), PDF p. 341 / printed p. 330, verified against the page image: with the 10RM load, rest about 5 minutes, do 5 reps, measure HR (F1); rest another 5 minutes, do 8-10 reps, measure HR (F2). PWC-170 = N1 + (N2 - N1)(170 - F1)/(F2 - F1), where N = 9.8 x W x R x D, and D is the bar distance as a fraction of lifter height H (Table 6.5). The squat "is far more commonly used." Table 6.5 values (concentric D / equivalent D for total work): full back squat 0.35 H / 0.60 H; half squat 0.22 / 0.37; bench press 0.28 / 0.56; squat clean 0.67 / 1.26; split clean 0.55 / 0.77; clean pull 0.50 / 0.50; snatch pull 0.59 / 0.59; power clean 0.65 / 0.69; deep good morning 0.35 / 0.52; jerk from chest 0.54 / 0.60; split snatch 0.67 / 0.89.

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning: a lower HR response to the same submaximal squat effort means higher work capacity (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329). No physiological explanation beyond that is given.

**When to apply** — As a low-cost in-house readiness and capacity check during a strength block, using an exercise athletes already do. Inference: no line in `docs/method-baseline.md` describes a lift-specific heart-rate response, so the Novik test would add to Baylor's force-plate and GPS monitoring rather than replace any of it.

**When NOT to apply** — The Novik test requires a measured 1RM squat, which the baseline says is not routinely tested (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material), citing Q10). Table 6.5 is not internally consistent with its own note: the text says eccentric action was "estimated to add 70% more work in each case where there is significant eccentric action," but the table's ratios differ (Inference from the printed values: back squat about +71%, bench press +100%, squat clean about +88%, power clean about +6%, pulls 0%). The book does not explain the variation. HR is also raised by "emotional arousal," so a high reading does not by itself separate fatigue from nerves.

**Example** — The authors' own: a weightlifter squats 3 reps at 85-90% of 1RM at intervals through a cycle; falling immediate and 1-minute post-set HR signals higher work capacity and permits more load (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329).

# The Periodisation Controversy: Verkhoshansky's Critique of Classical Periodisation and Zheljazkov's Reply

**What it is** — Section 6.3 (PDF p. 344-346 / printed p. 333-335; verified against the page images) is Siff's voice by the book's own signals: it names Verkhoshansky in the third person throughout and refers to what "this textbook introduced." It has three voices.

**Siff's framing.** Classical Matveyev periodisation is widely used in the West, yet "even among Russian researchers and scientists, this approach to training has attracted some fierce criticism." Siff accepts part of it: the belief that periodisation is "an exact science" with computerised prescriptions is wrong, because "The body is not an exactly controlled, deterministic system"; training is "as much a matter of art, trial-and-error, and intuition, as it is of science," so schemes "should serve as approximate guidelines" modified by physiological and psychological markers (PDF p. 344 / printed p. 333). He concludes "organising training according to the classical model of Matveyev can be used only by athletes of low qualification for certain phases of the programme," the reason the book introduced ongoing subjective and objective assessment (PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334). He also objects that classical computation "utilises only two factors," volume and intensity.

**Verkhoshansky (1997), as reported by Siff.** Periodisation "is not a suitable model for training for elite sportsmen" and should be "rejected or modified" for modern crowded calendars; "at best, separate forms of periodisation should be used by novice and young athletes." The mechanical division into periods and mesocycles rests on 1950s Soviet experience "mainly on the example of three sports, namely swimming, weightlifting, track and field athletics." Training should rest "much more on physiology." Plans should meet demands "distributed throughout a competitive season" rather than "notorious peaks of sports form." Kenyan runners "have never implemented periodisation"; British runners declined after adopting "Matveyev's block scheme" widely after 1980 (citing Horwill 1992, 1995; Tschiene 1991, 1992). He rejects "laws" of training and dismisses "'undulating models and 'wave models'" as "word play" (PDF p. 344-345 / printed p. 333-334).

**Zheljazkov (1998), as reported by Siff.** Periodisation "still managed to be utilised very effectively for many years in training numerous elite soviet and Eastern European athletes"; it is "erroneous" to treat Matveyev's concept as "the complete theory of sports training"; Verkhoshansky's charges of "primitive methodology" and "scholastic demagogy" are "a unprofessional personal attack"; national rises and falls in running are natural, not caused by periodisation. Classical periodisation "has not lost its fundamental importance" but has "serious qualitative limitations" to be modified by research on "exhaustion, adaptation and restoration," since regeneration is "nonlinear and heterochronical"; applied sport science "does not at all replace the entire concept of periodisation, but enriches it" (PDF p. 345-346 / printed p. 334-335).

**Why it works** — Each side argues from different evidence: Verkhoshansky from the 1950s origins of the model, its three-sport base and national running records; Zheljazkov from decades of Soviet and Eastern European elite success. Neither gives controlled data on these pages, and both national-results arguments are correlational (Inference).

**When to apply** — When a plan treats the annual chart as fixed. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred (transcript)), and "in football you want to peak every Saturday" (line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: both sides would accept the roadmap framing, and Verkhoshansky's season-long demands point fits weekly football games better than a single peak.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** Same question (is classical periodisation suitable for elite athletes), two named authorities, opposite answers, on PDF p. 344 versus p. 345. Note the internal tension with the book's own method: Verkhoshansky dismisses "undulating models" as word play (PDF p. 345), while the authors endorse heavy, medium and light alternation (PDF p. 326, 329); Inference: his complaint is about relabelling, not about load variation working, so it is a tension in emphasis, not a contradiction. This also touches Eric's baseline directly: "Undulating/non-linear periodization ... is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression" (line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Library sources: Issurin 2016 judged evidence for Verkhoshansky's own concentrated-unidirectional alternative insufficient for team sports ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]); Harries et al. 2015 found linear and undulating programmes give similar strength gains, and Afonso et al. 2019 argue that periodised-versus-non-periodised meta-analyses did not isolate periodisation's effect (vault research-papers entries). Inference: the modern papers support neither side's strong claim. # The Periodisation Controversy: Verkhoshansky's Critique of Classical Periodisation and Zheljazkov's Reply

**What it is** — Section 6.3 (PDF p. 344-346 / printed p. 333-335; verified against the page images) is Siff's voice by the book's own signals: it names Verkhoshansky in the third person throughout and refers to what "this textbook introduced." It has three voices.

He also objects that classical computation "utilises only two factors," volume and intensity.

**Verkhoshansky (1997), as reported by Siff.** Periodisation "is not a suitable model for training for elite sportsmen" and should be "rejected or modified" for modern crowded calendars; "at best, separate forms of periodisation should be used by novice and young athletes." The mechanical division into periods and mesocycles rests on 1950s Soviet experience "mainly on the example of three sports, namely swimming, weightlifting, track and field athletics." Training should rest "much more on physiology." Plans should meet demands "distributed throughout a competitive season" rather than "notorious peaks of sports form." Kenyan runners "have never implemented periodisation"; British runners declined after adopting "Matveyev's block scheme" widely after 1980 (Verkhoshansky's own claim). He cites Horwill (1992, 1995) condemning "the slavish worship of the theory of periodisation as used by some runners in different countries", and Tschiene (1991, 1992) concluding that "periodisation has not changed from the moment of Matveyev's first formalisation of the topic in 1965" and that "many coach's doctrines have not advanced" (PDF p. 344 / printed p. 333). He rejects "laws" of training and dismisses "'undulating models and 'wave models'" as "word play" (PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334). He also observes that "the general paradigm of periodisation was based heavily upon the philosophies and methodologies of communism": its cyclical nature "was strongly influenced by the 'five year plans' and other cycles of productivity in the soviet system," and "the precise calculation of training quantities reflected attempts to minimise the unscientific factors of subjectivity and emotiveness" (PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334).

**Zheljazkov (1998), as reported by Siff.** Periodisation "still managed to be utilised very effectively for many years in training numerous elite soviet and Eastern European athletes"; it is "erroneous" to treat Matveyev's concept as "the complete theory of sports training"; Verkhoshansky's charges of "primitive methodology" and "scholastic demagogy" are "a unprofessional personal attack"; national rises and falls in running are natural, not caused by periodisation. # The Periodisation Controversy: Verkhoshansky's Critique of Classical Periodisation and Zheljazkov's Reply

He concludes "organising training according to the classical model of Matveyev can be used only by athletes of low qualification for certain phases of the programme," the reason the book introduced ongoing subjective and objective assessment (PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334). He also objects that classical computation "utilises only two factors," volume and intensity.

**Verkhoshansky (1997), as reported by Siff.** Periodisation "is not a suitable model for training for elite sportsmen" and should be "rejected or modified" for modern crowded calendars; "at best, separate forms of periodisation should be used by novice and young athletes." The mechanical division into periods and mesocycles rests on 1950s Soviet experience "mainly on the example of three sports, namely swimming, weightlifting, track and field athletics." Training should rest "much more on physiology." Plans should meet demands "distributed throughout a competitive season" rather than "notorious peaks of sports form." Kenyan runners "have never implemented periodisation"; British runners declined after adopting "Matveyev's block scheme" widely after 1980 (Verkhoshansky's own claim). He cites Horwill (1992, 1995) condemning "the slavish worship of the theory of periodisation as used by some runners in different countries", and Tschiene (1991, 1992) concluding that "periodisation has not changed from the moment of Matveyev's first formalisation of the topic in 1965" and that "many coach's doctrines have not advanced" (PDF p. 344 / printed p. 333).
