It concludes only that "The possible link to periodisation of physical training then becomes apparent" (PDF p. 346 / printed p. 335). The text gives no study linking circadian mechanisms to multi-week or annual training cycles; Inference: a 24-hour clock says nothing direct about mesocycle or macrocycle length.

**Siff's framing.** Classical Matveyev periodisation is widely used in the West, yet "even among Russian researchers and scientists, this approach to training has attracted some fierce criticism." Siff accepts part of it: the belief that periodisation is "an exact science" with computerised prescriptions is wrong, because "The body is not an exactly controlled, deterministic system"; training is "as much a matter of art, trial-and-error, and intuition, as it is of science," so schemes "should serve as approximate guidelines" modified by physiological and psychological markers (PDF p. 344 / printed p. 333). He concludes "organising training according to the classical model of Matveyev can be used only by athletes of low qualification for certain phases of the programme," the reason the book introduced ongoing subjective and objective assessment (PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334). He also objects that classical computation "utilises only two factors," volume and intensity.

**Verkhoshansky (1997), as reported by Siff.** Periodisation "is not a suitable model for training for elite sportsmen" and should be "rejected or modified" for modern crowded calendars; "at best, separate forms of periodisation should be used by novice and young athletes." The mechanical division into periods and mesocycles rests on 1950s Soviet experience "mainly on the example of three sports, namely swimming, weightlifting, track and field athletics." Training should rest "much more on physiology." Plans should meet demands "distributed throughout a competitive season" rather than "notorious peaks of sports form." Kenyan runners "have never implemented periodisation"; British runners declined after adopting "Matveyev's block scheme" widely after 1980 (Verkhoshansky's own claim). He cites Horwill (1992, 1995) condemning "the slavish worship of the theory of periodisation as used by some runners in different countries", and Tschiene (1991, 1992) concluding that "periodisation has not changed from the moment of Matveyev's first formalisation of the topic in 1965" and that "many coach's doctrines have not advanced" (PDF p. 344 / printed p. 333). He rejects "laws" of training and dismisses "'undulating models and 'wave models'" as "word play" (PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334). He also observes that "the general paradigm of periodisation was based heavily upon the philosophies and methodologies of communism": its cyclical nature "was strongly influenced by the 'five year plans' and other cycles of productivity in the soviet system," and "the precise calculation of training quantities reflected attempts to minimise the unscientific factors of subjectivity and emotiveness" (PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334).

**Zheljazkov (1998), as reported by Siff.** Periodisation "still managed to be utilised very effectively for many years in training numerous elite soviet and Eastern European athletes"; it is "erroneous" to treat Matveyev's concept as "the complete theory of sports training"; Verkhoshansky's charges of "primitive methodology" and "scholastic demagogy" are "a unprofessional personal attack"; national rises and falls in running are natural, not caused by periodisation. On the communism point he partly agrees: "models of society such as communism indeed have a profound impact on the nature of sports training, but ... this happens in all countries and should not necessarily be taken to mean that this interaction between sport and society is always negative" (PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334). Classical periodisation "has not lost its fundamental importance" but has "serious qualitative limitations" to be modified by research on "exhaustion, adaptation and restoration," since regeneration is "nonlinear and heterochronical"; applied sport science "does not at all replace the entire concept of periodisation, but enriches it" (PDF p. 345-346 / printed p. 334-335).

**Chronobiology, the section's closing argument.** The subsection "Chronobiology and Periodisation" (PDF p. 346-347 / printed p. 335-336, verified against the page image of PDF 346) offers biological clocks as possible support: "Future corroboration of the principles of periodisation may rely on some of the advances being made in the field of chronobiology." The text describes a master circadian pacemaker, the suprachiasmatic nucleus, "entrained to the cycle of day and night by nervous input from the retina," which "can also be shifted or entrained by other stimuli, such as an appropriately timed bouts of exercise"; two further inputs, "one from the thalamic intergeniculate structure, and another from the midbrain raphe nuclei," "appear to play an important role in entraining or shifting rhythms by means of exercise and emotional arousal." It concludes only that "The possible link to periodisation of physical training then becomes apparent" (PDF p. 346 / printed p. 335). This is the section's only physiological argument for cycled training. Confidence for this part: `untested`. The text gives no study linking circadian mechanisms to multi-week or annual training cycles; Inference: a 24-hour clock says nothing direct about mesocycle or macrocycle length.

**Why it works** — Each side argues from different evidence: Verkhoshansky from the 1950s origins of the model, its three-sport base and national running records; Zheljazkov from decades of Soviet and Eastern European elite success. Neither gives controlled data on these pages, and both national-results arguments are correlational (Inference).

**When to apply** — When a plan treats the annual chart as fixed. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred (transcript)), and "in football you want to peak every Saturday" (line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: both sides would accept the roadmap framing, and Verkhoshansky's season-long demands point fits weekly football games better than a single peak.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** Same question (is classical periodisation suitable for elite athletes), two named authorities, opposite answers, on PDF p. 344 versus p. 345. Note the internal tension with the book's own method: Verkhoshansky dismisses "undulating models" as word play (PDF p. 345), while the authors endorse heavy, medium and light alternation (PDF p. 326, 329); Inference: his complaint is about relabelling, not about load variation working, so it is a tension in emphasis, not a contradiction. This also touches Eric's baseline directly: "Undulating/non-linear periodization ... is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression" (line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Library sources: Issurin 2016 judged evidence for Verkhoshansky's own concentrated-unidirectional alternative insufficient for team sports ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]); Harries et al. 2015 found linear and undulating programmes give similar strength gains, and Afonso et al. 2019 argue that periodised-versus-non-periodised meta-analyses did not isolate periodisation's effect (vault research-papers entries). Inference: the modern papers support neither side's strong claim. Evans frames the same split as "classic" versus "non-classic" literature ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--periodization-evidence-classic-vs-nonclassic-literature-debate]]).

**Example** — The authors' own: Verkhoshansky's claim that British runners "who used the Russian concept of periodisation did not gain gold medals on Olympic games over the last 30 years, but produced great achievements before they used such concepts," having adopted Matveyev's scheme widely after 1980, against Zheljazkov's reply that "all sports in all nations naturally undergo periods of ascendancy and decline" (PDF p. 344-345 / printed p. 333-334).

**Related** — [[framework--eight-weaknesses-of-the-matveyev-model]], [[principle--programming-is-an-art-on-principles-not-an-algorithm]], [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]], [[framework--six-broad-periodisation-schemes]], [[claim--heavy-medium-light-alternation-beats-monotonic-increasing-loading]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]], [[research-papers/harries-2015-systematic-review-and-meta-analysis-of-linear-and-undulating-periodized-resistance-trainin]], [[research-papers/afonso-2019-a-systematic-review-of-meta-analyses-comparing-periodized-and-non-periodized-exercise-prog]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--periodization-evidence-classic-vs-nonclassic-literature-debate]], [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--multi-peak-annual-preparation-elite-track-and-field]]
